title: Start Emberwire: message model, property expressions, v1 flow parser
body:
Node-RED is the heaviest thing in the App Store catalogue by an order of
magnitude and it looks like somebody else's product bolted into our dashboard.
This is the replacement, in Go. Same idea, our runtime, our editor.

Flow files stay Node-RED v1 compatible so nobody loses work on import.
Everything else is up for grabs.

What is here:

- Property expressions (property.go). The same grammar Node-RED's
  normalisePropertyExpression accepts, including nested forms like
  payload[msg.index], because every flow in existence encodes paths in it.
  Fuzzed, 4.3M execs clean. The msg. prefix inside brackets is stripped at
  resolve time, not parse time, so the editor echoes back exactly what was
  typed.

- Messages (msg.go). Deep clone on every fan-out. Node-RED hands the first
  recipient on a wire the original object and clones only for the ones after
  it, which means the last branch wired shares mutable state with the sender.
  That is a documented memory optimisation and an undocumented source of
  aliasing bugs. We do not copy it. The cost is bought back with
  ImmutableBytes, a shared-not-copied path for large binary payloads:
  measured 341ns vs 217us on a 1MB payload, 360B allocated instead of 1MB.
  Clone is cycle-safe and depth-bounded, because a function node can write
  msg.self = msg in one line and messages arrive from MQTT and HTTP bodies.

- Flow parser (flow.go). The v1 flat array, where a tab is a node, a subflow
  is a node and a group is a node. Config nodes detected structurally, no
  registry needed. Dangling wires and missing groups are warnings, not
  failures, because Node-RED loads those and refusing to would make a
  half-pasted flow unopenable. Unknown node types round-trip with every
  property intact, which is what makes it safe to run a Node-RED flow here
  and hand it back.

One thing I could not deliver as originally spec'd: byte-identical
round-trip. Go maps are unordered and encoding/json sorts keys, so the first
save after an import reorders keys once. Every save after that is
byte-identical, which is what actually matters for PVC and git churn. There
is a test pinning that.

title: Scheduler, node contract, and context stores
body:
The runtime model, which is where this stops being a Node-RED clone and
starts being a better one.

Scheduling. Node-RED runs everything on one event loop with a setImmediate
between every wire hop, so a five-node chain yields to the loop five times
and a CPU-heavy function stalls the editor, the HTTP endpoints and every
other flow on the box. Here each node instance gets its own goroutine and
its own bounded inbox. Ordered within a node, so a node keeps state across
messages with no locking. Parallel across nodes, which Node-RED cannot do
at all.

Back-pressure. This is the headline. Node-RED's send queue is an unbounded
setImmediate chain: a fast source outruns a slow sink until the pod dies
(node-red#855, open since 2016). Inboxes here are bounded with a policy per
node - block, drop-newest, drop-oldest, or raise to a Catch node. Block is
the default because it is the only one that loses nothing. A flow graph is
allowed to contain a cycle, so blocking is bounded by a timeout; otherwise a
ring of saturated inboxes deadlocks forever. Every drop is counted and
announced, because silently discarding a message is how a flow looks healthy
while losing data.

Catch/Status/Complete routing with the group-distance rule: a Catch inside a
group beats a Catch on the tab, uncaught handlers only fire when nothing
else took it, and a Catch wired back into the flow it catches for hits a hop
limit instead of spinning a core forever.

Node contract. One definition per node type, in Go. A Descriptor carries
everything the editor needs to render an edit dialog, so there is no
per-node HTML anywhere in this repo - Node-RED needs a hand-written .html
twin for every .js and the two drift. Descriptors are validated at
registration, so a malformed one fails the build rather than a deploy.
Every node must declare its compatibility level and explain any divergence:
a node that is 90% compatible and silent about it is worse than one that is
obviously missing.

Context stores with CompareAndSwap, Increment and Update. Node-RED offers
get and set, and FlowFuse names that gap as the specific reason a Node-RED
flow cannot be run in more than one instance - two copies doing
get-modify-set on a counter race and there is no primitive to fix it with.
Tested under 10,000 concurrent increments with zero lost updates.

Two shutdown races found and fixed while writing the tests, both of the kind
that kill a pod rather than fail a test:

- Closing a node's inbox on stop panicked when an async node called Send
  during shutdown. The inbox is never closed now; shutdown signals through a
  separate channel, which keeps the send path lock-free and makes a late
  Send harmless.
- The event channel was closed under one mutex while the guard flag was read
  under another. Both are under one lock now.

Measured on this box: 6.8us per message through a five-node chain, 14
allocs. Cloning is essentially all of it - Clone is 1.43us and there are
five hops - which is the price of giving every recipient its own copy
instead of aliasing the first one like Node-RED does. I will take that
trade and I have the numbers to revisit it if it ever matters.

Race detector runs in CI on Linux. It needs cgo and there is no gcc on my
Windows box, so I have not run it locally - that is what the ubuntu job is
for.

title: Survivable storage: atomic flow writes, AES-GCM credentials, crash recovery
body:
The "survives its own pod" requirement, done properly.

Flow file writes are atomic: temp file, fsync, rename, fsync the directory.
Every step earns its place. Node-RED writes flows.json in place, so a pod
evicted mid-write leaves a truncated file, and a truncated flow file means
the plant does not come back up. Test drives 200 writes alternating between
40 bytes and 200KB with a reader hammering the file, and asserts the reader
never once sees invalid JSON.

Backups rotate three deep, because atomic writes protect against a torn file
and not against a wrong one - a deploy that saves a valid but incorrect flow
set is just as much a loss. If the primary file will not parse, Load walks
the backups newest-first, keeps the bad file as .corrupt for forensics, and
puts a warning on the flow set so the operator actually finds out. Starting
empty on a corrupt file would look like a clean boot and silently bin every
flow the customer had. If nothing is readable it refuses to start, because
there is nothing honest to do at that point.

Revisions are content-derived, not a counter. Two editor tabs open on one
runtime cannot silently overwrite each other, and a restart does not reset
the token and let a stale tab clobber newer work.

Credentials move to AES-256-GCM keyed with Argon2id. Node-RED uses
AES-256-CTR keyed with a raw SHA-256 of the secret. Neither has a CVE and
both are real problems: CTR has no MAC, so anyone who can write the file on
a shared PVC can flip chosen plaintext bits and turn "can write a file" into
"can change a broker password to one they know"; and plain SHA-256 is not a
KDF, it is fast by design, which is the opposite of what you want between a
stolen file and a weak passphrase. There is a test that flips one bit and
asserts the file no longer opens. The format string is authenticated as
additional data so it cannot be rewritten to steer at a weaker scheme.

Node-RED's format is still readable, because refusing to import an existing
deployment's credentials makes migration impossible. Read-only - anything
loaded that way is re-encrypted under GCM on the next save. The test builds
a real Node-RED credential file with CTR and SHA-256 and imports it.

Also handles the __PWRD__ sentinel the editor sends for a password field it
displayed but did not touch. Treating that as a new value would overwrite
every password with the literal string the first time anyone opened an edit
dialog.

One real bug found by the tests: runners stop concurrently, so a downstream
node could drain its inbox to empty and exit while an upstream node still
had messages to forward - the work went into a channel nobody was reading
any more and vanished. Shutdown now waits for every node to be
simultaneously idle before signalling anyone to quit, bounded by the close
timeout so one runaway cycle cannot hold up a deploy forever. That makes
"a redeploy finishes work in flight" true rather than usually-true.

Two Windows notes, neither a compromise of the Linux guarantee. Chmod there
only toggles read-only, so the permissions test is Linux-only. And Windows
refuses to rename over a file any handle has open, so the concurrent-reader
test cannot even set up its scenario there - I skipped it rather than
weakening the test or the write path to make a Windows limitation disappear.
Both run on ubuntu in CI, which is what the binary actually ships on.

title: Core nodes: inject, debug, change, switch, range, filter, link, catch/status/complete
body:
First wave of the palette, plus the typed-input machinery underneath it.

TypedInput is the thing that makes flows composable in the first place: any
field can hold a literal, a message property, a context lookup or an
environment variable, and the node does not care which. Node-RED spells the
type discriminator differently on nearly every node - pt, tot, vt, fromt, v2t
- so it is declared per property rather than guessed. Context keys split
correctly too: flow.get("a.b") reads property b of what is stored under "a",
not a key literally named "a.b".

Nested context writes go through Update rather than get-then-set, so two
nodes writing different sub-paths of the same key do not lose each other's
changes. That is the atomic primitive from the last commit earning its keep.

Deliberate refusals, all tested:

- JSONata-typed values error instead of being ignored. Returning the
  expression text would make a flow appear to work while setting a property
  to a literal string, which is the worst possible outcome.
- Switch rejects jsonata_exp rules at build time.
- Filter refuses narrowband modes rather than quietly behaving like
  something else.
- Link Out errors when a target is not running. Node-RED drops these
  silently, which makes a mistyped or deleted link target very hard to find.
- Range refuses an empty input range - dividing by a zero span yields
  infinity and poisons everything downstream.

Two correctness details worth calling out.

Numeric strings are not coerced against each other in comparisons. "01" and
"1" are both numeric-looking but they are not the same string, and coercing
them would route two different zero-padded device ids down the same branch.
Coercion only kicks in when at least one side is genuinely a number.

Range multiplies before dividing. The obvious ordering computes a fraction
first, and 1.1 is not representable, so mapping 11 from 0..10 onto 0..100
lands on 110.00000000000001 and a wrap yields 10.000000000000014. Nobody
wants that on a dashboard. Caught by a test, not by luck.

Every descriptor declares a compatibility level, and there is a test that
fails the build if a node claims partial compatibility without saying in
writing what is missing. A node that is 90% compatible and quiet about it is
more dangerous than one that is obviously absent.

title: Sequence nodes, README, and a compatibility matrix that cannot go stale
body:
split, join, sort and batch, plus the msg.parts machinery they share. Field
names match Node-RED exactly, so a sequence produced here is joinable by a
Node-RED Join node and the reverse, and a function node inspecting parts
sees what it expects.

Object splits emit keys in sorted order. Go map iteration is randomised, so
without that the same flow produces a different sequence on every run -
which looks fine in testing and ruins a report in production.

String splits by length work in runes, not bytes. The plant floor has degree
signs and accented names in it, and byte-splitting UTF-8 breaks a character
at every boundary.

Join keys on the sequence id, so two Split nodes feeding one Join do not
blend into each other. There is a test that interleaves two sequences
deliberately.

Batch with overlap clones the shared messages, otherwise the second group
carries the first group's parts.

Found a real bug while testing sort: compare() coerced numeric-looking
strings to numbers even when both sides were strings, so ["10","9","100"]
sorted numerically without anyone asking. In JavaScript "10" < "9" is true,
because two strings compare lexically no matter how numeric they look. This
also affected switch - a flow routing on a zero-padded device id would have
gone down the wrong branch. Coercion now only applies when at least one side
is genuinely a number, which is the case that actually matters since edit
dialogs persist numeric fields as strings. Regression tests on both nodes.

The compatibility matrix is generated from the registry, not written by
hand, and a test fails when the file on disk drifts from what the code
declares. A hand-maintained matrix goes stale the moment someone adds a node
in a hurry, and a stale compatibility claim is worse than none - it is the
document a customer reads before deciding whether their flow will work. The
only way to change what it says is to change what the code says.

17 node types: 8 full, 9 partial, every partial one explaining itself.

README says plainly what is done, what is not, and what I have not measured
yet. The Node-RED comparison numbers are not in there because I have not run
the harness, and the RSS and throughput figures on the forums are anecdotes
with no controlled measurement behind them. They go in when I produce them
myself on the same box with the same flow, and not before.

title: Byte-identical flow file round-trip
body:
I said this was not achievable in the last pass. That was wrong, and it was
me taking the easy path rather than an actual constraint.

What is true: a JavaScript object preserves key insertion order, so Node-RED
gets a byte-identical round-trip for free out of JSON.parse and
JSON.stringify. A Go map has no order and encoding/json deliberately sorts
keys. What I concluded from that - that the goal was out of reach - only
rules out the naive approach.

Each entry's original bytes are now kept alongside the parsed map. On save,
an entry that still deep-equals what was read is written back verbatim.
json.Compact and json.Indent are byte-level transforms, so they re-indent
without touching key order. Equality is checked by decoding the original
rather than by a dirty flag, because a dirty flag depends on every mutation
site remembering to set it and the one that forgets is the one that
corrupts a customer's file.

An entry that did change is re-encoded against the original key order rather
than sorted, recursing through nested objects and arrays - a Change node's
rules, a Switch node's rules, all the structure that actually matters is
nested. Without that, editing one property rewrote all fourteen lines of the
node. Now it is one line. Verified:

    line 24
      - "topic": "press/01/raw",
      + "topic": "press/01/scaled",

Also turned off Go's HTML escaping. encoding/json rewrites <, > and & as
\u003c and friends; JSON.stringify does not. Leaving it on would have
rewritten every template and every URL query in a customer's file on the
first save. There is a fixture with an HTML template in it and a test that
forces the re-encode path.

Two reasons this earns its keep. The flow file lives on a PVC and in git and
should not churn because a pod restarted. And when an operator reviews a
deploy diff before pushing it to a line, they need to see what changed and
nothing else.

New fixture in Node-RED's exact JSON.stringify(flows, null, 4) output
format, and four tests: byte-identical round-trip, key order is source order
and not alphabetical, no rewritten escapes, and a one-property edit produces
a one-line diff.

title: It runs. Config, admin API, websocket, and the binary
body:
emberwire now starts, serves an API, runs flows and persists them. Verified
end to end on a real flow: 4-20mA reading -> range scale -> switch on a
threshold -> change tags ALARM or OK -> debug -> websocket frame in a client.
Restarted the process and the flow came back off disk with zero failures.

Configuration is declarative YAML with environment overrides. Node-RED's
settings.js is executable JavaScript - adminAuth can be a function, https can
be a function, storageModule is a require() - which makes it impossible to
validate, diff, or template from a ConfigMap without running it. This is a
struct, and unknown keys are a startup error rather than a setting that
silently does nothing. An operator who misspells credentialSecret finds out
immediately instead of when they discover the file is plaintext.

Two things it refuses to do, both with the remedy printed:

  refusing to start: authentication is enabled but no users are configured.
  Generate a hash with: emberwire hash-password

  refusing to start: no credential secret is set, so node credentials would
  be written to disk in plaintext.

The first is CVE-2025-41656 - unauthenticated RCE against a default Node-RED
config, by deploying a flow with an exec node in it. Node-RED's own team
proposed exactly this fix in designs#81 and did not ship it. Override with
EMBERWIRE_INSECURE=true if you are genuinely on an isolated network, but you
have to say so out loud.

Passwords are bcrypt only. A plaintext password in auth.users is rejected at
startup so one cannot end up in a ConfigMap by accident. Login runs the hash
comparison even for an unknown username, so response timing does not reveal
which accounts exist.

The comms websocket fixes two things I did not want to inherit. Node-RED's
unsubscribe handler is a stub - its source says "all clients get
automatically subscribed to everything and cannot unsubscribe" - so every
open editor receives every debug message from every flow on the box. Here a
client subscribes to what it wants and unsubscribe is honoured. And a client
that falls behind is disconnected rather than allowed to accumulate an
unbounded queue: a browser tab left open on a laptop lid must not be able to
affect a production line. Events go out in batches of up to 64 frames.

Deploy order is deliberate and not the obvious one. Credentials are split out
and the flow file is written BEFORE the old runtime is stopped, so a failure
to persist leaves the previous flows running rather than taking the line down
for a bad save. Context belonging to deleted nodes and flows is swept on each
deploy so redeploying does not accumulate state for things that are gone.

emberwire import prints a compatibility report before anyone deploys
anything - what is supported, what is partial and why, what will not start.
Finding that out now beats finding it out when a line stops.

Found a real bug doing this. The debug node reached the editor through a
package-level function variable that nothing ever assigned, so every publish
was skipped by a nil check. It compiled, every test passed, and the sidebar
was silently empty. Publishing is on the Emitter now, which means it is wired
by construction and cannot be unwired, and there is a test that fails if it
ever is. Also caught that my node test harness hand-built engine.Node and
skipped the parser, which is how the gap hid - the harness goes through
ParseFlows now like a real deploy does.

Binary is 11MB on Windows before -ldflags "-s -w".

title: Database export, MQTT, and parsers
body:
The point of this thing on a plant floor: read a sensor, shape the data,
write it to a historian. That path works now.

Databases, targeting what is actually in the App Store catalogue:

- postgres, covering postgresql-app AND timescale-db-pod. TimescaleDB is a
  PostgreSQL extension speaking the identical wire protocol, so one node
  serves both. Insert mode maps columns from message properties; query mode
  runs SQL with positional parameters and returns rows on msg.payload.
- influxdb out, targeting influxdb-app. Line protocol over HTTP rather than
  a client library - the protocol is small and stable, and a client would
  add weight to the binary to save eighty lines. Handles 1.8 and 2.x.

pgx and paho are both pure Go, so CGO_ENABLED=0 and distroless still hold.
Binary is 17.6MB before -ldflags "-s -w".

Two things I was careful about, because getting them wrong fails silently
rather than loudly.

Line protocol escaping. The rules differ by position - measurement, tag
key/value, field key, string field value - and getting it wrong does not
error. It writes the point under a mangled series name, or splits one series
in two because a tag value had a space in it, and you find out weeks later
when a dashboard is missing half its data. Tested against quotes,
backslashes, commas and spaces in every position. An unresolved tag is
omitted rather than written empty, because InfluxDB indexes on the tag set
and an empty string is a different series.

Numbers go to InfluxDB as floats even when whole. InfluxDB stores int and
float as distinct types and rejects a later write that disagrees with the
first, so a sensor reporting 21 and then 21.5 would fail on the second.

SQL identifiers are validated, not trusted. Table and column names cannot be
parameterised so they get concatenated into the statement, and they come
from an edit dialog reachable by anyone who can deploy a flow. "They already
have exec" is not a reason to hand out a second injection path. Values are
always parameters. Tested against the obvious payloads.

Both config nodes connect lazily rather than at deploy. A database or broker
that is not up yet must not stop the flow from starting - on an edge box
they boot together, and failing a node at deploy time over a transient
connection error is why people wrap Node-RED in restart loops.

MQTT in/out against monster-mq. Subscriptions are recorded and replayed on
reconnect so behaviour is the same whether clean session is on or off, which
matters because an edge link drops constantly. Client id defaults to one
derived from the node id rather than random, so a reconnect after a restart
resumes the same session instead of orphaning it. auto payload mode parses
JSON and falls back to a string, and leaves a non-UTF8 payload as a buffer
rather than filling it with replacement characters.

json and csv parsers. CSV keeps a leading zero as a string - "007" is a
device id, not the number 7 - and emits rows as a stamped sequence so a
batching database insert downstream can reassemble them. Derived columns are
sorted, because Go map order is randomised and a CSV whose columns move
between rows is unusable.

Integration tests against real infrastructure are in, skipped unless the
environment says where to find it. There is no docker daemon on this box so
I have not run them - they are for ut3 against the real monster-mq,
influxdb-app and postgresql-app, command line is in the file header. Unit
tests cover the escaping and the SQL building; the integration tests cover
what unit tests cannot, like whether the broker likes our client id.

title: Helm chart with three network modes, Dockerfile, and the editor shell
body:
Emberwire is deployable now, and it has a UI.

The chart follows the App Store contract exactly. THE BIG FIVE store labels on
the pod AND the Service - ten rendered, and CI fails the publish if that number
moves, because labels on the pod alone make an app show in node detail and stay
invisible in Running Apps, which is the most common silent failure in the
catalogue and is not visible from reading the chart. name and fullname forced
to .Release.Name for FQDN proxy routing. storeAnnotations reads
.Values.embernet.displayName first and .Values.gui.displayName only as a
fallback - the other order silently drops the name the dashboard injects and
every node card shows the raw release name. tenantLabels on both. ClusterIP
8080 to 1880 with ClientIP session affinity, because the editor holds a
websocket and without affinity it is cut the moment there is more than one
endpoint. 2Gi PVC. Chart name has no "pod" in it.

Three network modes, and the third is the reason this project exists on a plant
floor:

  cluster  ClusterIP. Multi-instance safe, unlimited per node. Sees what the
           cluster routes. Default.
  host     hostNetwork. Sees the host's interfaces and broadcast domain.
           One instance per node, because the port is the node's.
  macvlan  Multus. The pod gets its own MAC and its own IP on the target VLAN.
           BOTH multi-instance safe AND sitting directly on the segment with
           the PLCs - no shared port space, so no collisions.

No other App Store chart ships macvlan. The MACVLAN-K3S-Implementation repo was
retired and its index never resolved, and the only Multus support in the
catalogue is in the KubeVirt MicroVM charts, which reference pre-existing
NetworkAttachmentDefinitions rather than creating them. This creates one.

Every bad configuration is refused at render time with the fix in the message -
unknown mode, macvlan without a subnet, macvlan referencing a NAD it does not
name, discovery enabled with no allowed CIDRs. CI asserts each guard actually
fires, because a guard that does not fire is worse than no guard: it reads as
validated.

The credential secret and the admin password are read back from the existing
Secret on upgrade rather than regenerated. This is not tidiness. If
credential-secret regenerates, every credential already encrypted onto the PVC
becomes undecryptable and every broker password in every flow is gone - and it
would look like a successful upgrade until somebody noticed their MQTT nodes
could not authenticate. A bare randAlphaNum would do exactly that on the first
helm upgrade.

Recreate rather than RollingUpdate: two pods cannot share a ReadWriteOnce PVC,
and if they could they would both subscribe to the same topics and both write
to the same historian.

Dockerfile is three stages - esbuild, Go, distroless/static - and fails the
build if the binary comes out dynamically linked, because that is a thing you
otherwise discover from a CrashLoopBackOff. Image publishes for amd64 and
arm64; the edge fleet is not all x86.

The editor shell is in and served from the binary via embed.FS. Vanilla
TypeScript, native DOM, zero dependencies at runtime - 8.9kb of JS and 6.4kb of
CSS, against Node-RED's several megabytes of jQuery, D3 and vendored Monaco.
Login, live runtime stats with a queue-depth meter per node, the event stream,
and the palette with each node's compatibility level on it.

Theme copies the dashboard's mechanism exactly: properties on :root, redefined
on body.dark-mode, localStorage with a prefers-color-scheme fallback, and an
inline head script so a dark-mode user never sees a white flash. It also listens
for a postMessage theme event from the parent frame, so toggling the dashboard's
theme moves the embedded app with it instead of leaving it on the other one.

Two things found while wiring it up. http.FileServer canonicalises a request for
index.html into a 301 back to the directory, and since the handler rewrites "/"
to index.html that is a redirect loop on the editor's own root - files are
served directly now. And content types are set explicitly rather than sniffed,
because Go's DetectContentType reads the first 512 bytes and a JS module
starting with a comment sniffs as text/plain, which a browser refuses to
execute.

Verified: editor at /, unknown routes fall back to index.html for client
routing, a missing .js still 404s instead of returning HTML with a 200, and the
API routes are not swallowed by the catch-all - /nodes still 401s without a
token and returns 26 node types with one.

The flow canvas is next. It goes on top of this same API client and this same
theme.

title: Network discovery: scan the OT segment, not just what k3s routes
body:
This is what the macvlan network mode exists to enable. A flow engine that can
only see what the cluster routes to it cannot inventory a plant floor; with its
own MAC and IP on the OT VLAN, it can.

Two nodes. netinfo reports the runtime's interfaces and addresses, which in
macvlan mode is how a flow learns the address it was given on the OT VLAN and
therefore what it should be sweeping. scan sweeps a CIDR for the ports that
actually matter on a plant floor - Modbus 502, OPC-UA 4840, EtherNet/IP 44818,
BACnet 47808, S7 102, Omron FINS 9600 - and identifies what answered.

Identification is read-only by construction. Modbus gets function 43 / MEI 14
Read Device Identification, which the spec defines as read-only and is the only
identification request that does not touch process data; a device that does not
implement it answers with an exception, which still confirms it speaks Modbus,
so an exception is a positive result here rather than a failure. EtherNet/IP
gets ListIdentity, command 0x0063, which is what every EtherNet/IP browser
sends. Nothing in this package writes to a device. A discovery scan that can
change a coil is not a discovery scan.

TCP connect rather than raw SYN. It needs no elevated capability, behaves the
same inside a container with capabilities dropped, and completes the handshake
instead of leaving half-open connections on a PLC whose TCP stack may have a
connection table of eight entries.

The safety boundary is the CIDR allowlist and it lives in operator
configuration, not in an edit dialog. These nodes are reachable by anyone who
can edit a flow, and "it is on an isolated network" stops being true the day
somebody bridges a VLAN. Specifics:

- Discovery disabled is the default, and a scan node in that state errors
  rather than returning nothing - an empty result looks exactly like a network
  with nothing on it.
- Enabled with no CIDRs is a configuration error, not "no restrictions". The
  permissive reading of an empty list is how a tool meant for one factory
  segment ends up scanning a corporate network.
- A range must sit ENTIRELY inside an allowed prefix. Overlap is not enough:
  sweeping 10.0.0.0/8 because 10.20.30.0/24 is permitted would defeat the whole
  thing, and an /8 sweep from an edge box is also a very effective way to take
  out an OT link.
- A hostname must have EVERY resolved address in scope, not any, or DNS becomes
  the way around the allowlist.
- Sweeps are capped at 4096 addresses. A /16 is 65,534, and letting one node
  enqueue that many probes would saturate a 100Mb link shared with the process
  traffic that matters. Concurrency defaults to 32 for the same reason - a
  discovery scan must never be why a line stutters.

Found a real protocol bug while testing. My Modbus device-identification parser
read the object count from byte 12, which is NextObjectId, not byte 13, which is
NumberOfObjects - so it parsed zero objects and reported no vendor, product code
or revision for every device that answered. Off by one, in a place where the
symptom is "discovery works but finds nothing useful" rather than a crash.
Caught by a test built from a real response layout, which is the only reason it
did not ship.

Results merge per address, so four probe types finding one device produce one
entry rather than four - otherwise an inventory of forty machines reads as a
hundred and sixty. Addresses sort numerically, not lexically, so .9 comes before
.10 the way anyone scanning a device list expects. Output is stable across
repeated scans of an unchanged network, so a downstream change filter does not
fire on nothing and page somebody at 3am for a change that did not happen.

Chart wires this up: discovery.enabled with discovery.allowedCIDRs, and
NET_RAW/NET_ADMIN added only when it is on. Without those capabilities the
scan degrades to TCP connect probing rather than failing.

28 node types now: 8 full, 14 partial, 6 Emberwire-only.

title: Function node on goja, and integration tests against real infrastructure
body:
Podman in WSL, as you said. Ran the whole thing against real mosquitto,
InfluxDB 2.7 and PostgreSQL 16 containers, and got the race detector as a
bonus - WSL has gcc, which my Windows box does not.

All three integration tests pass against real services. The one that matters
most: the InfluxDB tag value came back out of a real database as
"press 01,west" with the space and comma intact. That is the line-protocol
escaping I said would fail silently and fragment a series, now proven end to
end rather than against my own encoder.

Race detector: clean across every package, including the scheduler under ten
thousand concurrent context operations. I have been flagging that as unverified
all session. It is verified now.

The Function node runs on goja. Node's own documentation says the vm module
"is not a security mechanism" and must not be used for untrusted code; escapes
work by reaching a Function constructor and walking out to process and
child_process. goja has no host bindings at all unless you add them, so there
is nothing to walk to - the escape surface is exactly the list of things
host.go puts in the runtime, and there is a test asserting require, process,
module, Buffer and friends are all undefined. There is also a test that runs
the standard constructor-chain escape and asserts it reaches nothing.

Always a CPU ceiling. Node-RED's function timeout is optional and off by
default, so while(true){} spins a core until the pod is OOM-killed. Here the
interrupt fires and the message errors. Tested, including that cancelling the
context stops a running function so a shutdown does not wait on one.

No setTimeout or setInterval, deliberately. Work scheduled inside a function is
invisible to the scheduler, cannot be back-pressured, and outlives the message
that started it. A Delay or Trigger node does the same job where the runtime
can account for it.

Also exposed flow.incr and global.cas, which Node-RED has no equivalent of.
Same reason as before: get-modify-set on a shared counter loses updates and
there was no primitive to fix it with.

Two real bugs found, one of them nasty.

The nasty one: I named the file function_js.go, and Go treats _js as an
implicit GOOS build constraint for js/wasm. Both the node and its tests were
silently excluded from every build. go build ./... passed, go vet passed, the
full suite passed - and the Function node was simply not registered. I only
caught it because `go test -run TestFunction` said "no tests to run" and I
chased it instead of shrugging. Confirmed by the import report listing function
under "NOT supported". Renamed to jsfunction.go. Worth remembering: _linux,
_windows, _arm, _js and friends are all load-bearing filename suffixes.

The second: goja exports an integral number as int64 while everything else in
the runtime speaks JSON, where every number is float64 - a message off MQTT, a
row from PostgreSQL, a value from the flow file. Letting the Function node be
the one place emitting int64 means a payload of 42 compares, serialises and
stores differently depending on whether it went through JavaScript. Normalised
at every boundary out of the runtime.

Also fixed message id propagation: I checked for an existing id after calling
WrapMsg, which assigns one when absent, so the check always passed and the
original was lost. Tracing now survives a function that builds a fresh object,
which is most of them.

Measured: 21us per invocation, about 47k calls a second. Honest number for an
interpreter, and the compile happens once at deploy rather than per message.

Verified through the running binary: a two-output function with initialize code
and flow.incr, three messages in, correctly split one to alarm and two to ok.

title: The flow canvas
body:
Drag from the palette, wire nodes together, edit them, deploy. The editor is
a real editor now.

Native SVG and pointer events. Node-RED uses D3 for this; the parts actually
needed - a viewBox transform and some drag maths - are about forty lines, and
the library would cost more than it saves and would still have to be themed.
Whole editor is 34kb of JS and 12kb of CSS. Node-RED's is several megabytes of
jQuery, D3 and a vendored Monaco.

Edit dialogs are rendered from the node descriptor. This is the payoff for the
Descriptor work: in Node-RED every node type ships a hand-written .html twin
carrying its edit form, its help text and a registerType call, so adding a
property means editing markup in a second language and keeping two files in
step. Here a node declares typed properties in Go, the API serves them as
JSON, and dialog.ts renders a form. A new node type gets a working dialog with
no front-end change at all. Handles string, number, bool, select, typedInput
with its per-node type discriminator, config-node references, credentials,
code panes and repeatable rule lists.

Details that matter for actually using it:

- Undo checkpoints at the start of an interaction, not after each mutation, so
  dragging twenty nodes is one undo step rather than twenty.
- Nodes snap to the grid on release rather than continuously, so dragging feels
  smooth instead of stepping.
- Marquee select uses intersection, not containment - dragging a box across a
  row should catch it, not require enclosing it exactly.
- Zoom is about the cursor, so the thing under the pointer stays under it.
- Wire deletion is alt-click. Plain click would mean brushing past a wire while
  selecting silently breaks a flow.
- A backward wire bows wider, because a loop or a retry path is normal and the
  default curve doubles back through both nodes.
- Ports spread around a node's centre, so a three-output Switch reads
  symmetrically instead of hanging off the top edge.
- Ctrl+Enter saves a dialog; plain Enter would submit while somebody is halfway
  through typing a function body. Tab indents in a code pane rather than
  ejecting focus.
- Clicking a row in the runtime table selects that node on the canvas, which is
  how you get from "this node is erroring" to the node.
- A node type this runtime does not have renders grey with a dashed outline and
  its config editable as raw JSON, so a flow using something unimplemented is
  visibly wrong and repairable rather than silently missing pieces.
- Credentials show whether a value is stored, never the value, and send the
  unchanged sentinel when untouched. Without that, opening a dialog and pressing
  Done would blank every password.
- Status events paint badges on the canvas rather than filling the debug log,
  because one chatty node would otherwise drown out the output you asked for.
- beforeunload guard, because losing an afternoon of wiring to a stray Cmd-W is
  not a mistake anyone should be able to make once.
- A deploy conflict prompts rather than resolving itself. Overwriting silently
  would throw away somebody else's work; reloading silently would throw away
  yours.

Verified against the running binary: bundle served from the embedded FS, deploy
with the rev header round-trips, and a stale rev returns 409 with the two
revisions in the message rather than silently overwriting.

title: WASM guests: the sandbox that can actually bound memory
body:
goja is a good boundary - no host bindings unless you add them - but it cannot
limit memory. A JavaScript function allocating in a loop grows the Go heap
until the pod is OOM-killed, and a wall-clock timeout is the only defence.
WebAssembly has a linear memory with a declared maximum, so a guest that
allocates past its ceiling fails inside the guest and the host is untouched.

There is a test proving exactly that: a guest that allocates a megabyte a
million times gets stopped, and the very next message through the same module
returns the right answer. That is the guarantee, demonstrated rather than
claimed.

Also means a node can be written in Rust, TinyGo, Zig or AssemblyScript instead
of JavaScript, which matters for the signal processing an OT flow actually
wants to do.

wazero, so still pure Go, still CGO_ENABLED=0, still distroless. Binary is
20.5MB with goja AND wazero AND the editor embedded. nodered/node-red:latest is
about 450MB.

The ABI is three exports, two of them allocator hooks. A wide ABI is a wide
attack surface and every entry is something a guest author has to get right.
JSON over linear memory because a guest in any language can produce it without
a shared schema compiler. Guests get no filesystem, no network, no environment,
no preopened directories - WASI is instantiated so a TinyGo or Rust wasm32-wasi
binary starts at all, and it reaches nothing.

Things the host has to get right, each with a test:

- A trapped instance is never reused. A trap can leave the guest's allocator
  inconsistent, and handing that to the next message produces failures that
  look random and take a day to chase.
- The response is copied out of linear memory before the instance goes back in
  the pool. The returned slice aliases guest memory and the next call would
  overwrite it underneath us.
- A guest reporting a length past the end of its own memory gets an error, not
  a host read of something it should not see. Bounds-checked, plus an explicit
  output ceiling so a guest cannot make the host allocate by lying about size.
- Input goes through the guest's own allocator rather than being written
  wherever. Writing elsewhere corrupts whatever the guest believes it owns.
- Missing entry points fail at compile, not on the first message - the
  difference between a red node and a flow that quietly drops everything.
- Instances are pooled and the pool hands each caller its own, because a wazero
  instance is not safe for concurrent use and a config node shared by several
  nodes does not get the scheduler's one-at-a-time guarantee.

The reference guest is in testdata and is built by CI rather than committed - a
3MB binary artefact in the repo gets reviewed by nobody and drifts from the
source beside it. CI also asserts the sandbox tests actually RAN rather than
skipped, because a skipped test reads as a passing one in the summary and these
are the tests behind the security claims in the README.

Measured: 169us per guest call against 21us for goja. WASM is the heavier
option and it buys a hard memory ceiling; goja stays the default and this is
what you reach for when a node needs a real boundary or is not written in
JavaScript.

title: Prometheus metrics
body:
The README table claimed "Prometheus, per node" and the chart shipped a
ServiceMonitor pointing at an endpoint that did not exist. Rather than soften
the claim, built it.

Per-node message counts, error counts, drops, blocked sends and queue depth,
plus goroutines, heap and GC. Node-RED exposes nothing comparable, and the
queue high-water mark in particular is the difference between knowing a flow is
backing up and finding out when the kubelet kills the pod. The dropped and
blocked counters have no Node-RED equivalent at all, because its queue is
unbounded so there is nothing to count.

Hand-written rather than client_golang. The data is already atomics on each
node runner, the exposition format is small and stable, and the library would
add megabytes to a binary whose entire argument is that it is small. What the
library actually buys - label escaping, consistent HELP and TYPE, deterministic
output - is reproduced deliberately rather than skipped:

- Label values are escaped. A node's type comes out of a flow file anyone can
  write, and an unescaped quote or newline produces a scrape that silently
  fails to parse. The first symptom is a dashboard that quietly stops updating.
- Families are emitted with HELP and TYPE even when they have no series, so a
  dashboard on an idle runtime gets an empty result rather than an unknown
  metric - "no messages" and "monitoring is broken" must not look the same.
- Output is sorted, so two scrapes of an unchanged runtime are identical and a
  diff shows what changed rather than a reshuffle.

Unauthenticated, like /health. A Prometheus scraper carries no bearer token,
and requiring one means either handing a credential to the monitoring stack or
having no monitoring. The endpoint exposes counts and node ids, never message
contents or configuration.

Verified by scraping the running binary with a real flow: four messages into a
JavaScript function, correctly split two and two across its outputs, all
visible in the exposition.

title: Template, Delay and Trigger, and a scheduler that waits for timers
body:
Three of the four remaining function-category nodes. The fourth, exec, is
next and needs a config gate before it goes anywhere near a customer.

Template needed a Mustache engine, since Go has no standard-library one. It
is mustache.js's dialect rather than the specification's, deliberately: the
flows we have to run were written against Node-RED, which embeds mustache.js,
and two of its extensions change the bytes that come out.

  - The escape set includes "/", "=" and backtick. A template emitting a URL
    path through {{ }} comes out with / in Node-RED, and a flow may well
    be compensating for it already.
  - A section tag alone on a line takes the whole line with it. Without that
    every section leaves a blank line behind and a generated YAML or CSV
    document is malformed rather than merely untidy.

Partials and custom delimiters are refused rather than ignored — there is
nothing in a flow file that can supply either, so accepting them silently
would only produce a template that renders half of what it says.

Numbers render as JavaScript would: 5, not 5.000000. That one is not
cosmetic. A rendered SQL statement or MQTT topic carrying 5.000000 is wrong
in a way nobody notices until it is in a database.

Delay implements all six modes, including per-topic queue and timed release,
plus msg.reset, msg.flush and the second output. Two deliberate divergences,
both written into the compatibility matrix:

  - The queue is bounded. Node-RED's is not, which is node-red#855 wearing a
    different hat: a source faster than the drain grows the heap until the
    kubelet kills the pod and the flow author gets a restart with nothing in
    the log. Past the limit a message is refused to a Catch node, at the
    point the assumption actually broke.
  - A message the rate limiter chooses not to send leaves by the second
    output when there is one, and is counted and logged when there is not.
    Nothing goes missing quietly.

Trigger gets both messages, extend-on-retrigger, wait-to-be-reset, per-topic
grouping and the msg.delay override, under the same queue bound.

Both of them hold work that no inbox knows about, which broke an assumption
in the scheduler. quiesce judged a node idle on inbox depth and in-flight
count, so a Delay node holding fifty messages on timers looked quiet and the
runtime tore down around them — which is precisely what Node-RED does, and
the messages are simply gone. So node.Deferrer: a node reports what it is
holding, runner.idle consults it, and a redeploy waits. Cancellation happens
before the wait starts, so both nodes release early and the wait is short
rather than the full close timeout.

One judgement call in Trigger worth writing down: a timer with a deadline
fires early on shutdown, but a timer waiting to be reset is dropped. Firing
the first loses nothing; firing the second would invent an event that never
happened.

title: The exec node, behind a lock that Node-RED does not have
body:
This is the node behind CVE-2025-41656 — unauthenticated remote code
execution against a default Node-RED, reached by deploying a flow with an
exec node in it. The severity comes from there being nothing at all between
"can edit a flow" and "can run any command". Emberwire already refuses to
start without authentication, which closes the unauthenticated half. This
closes the other half.

Three things, and none of them is negotiable:

The node ships disabled. An operator lists the commands a flow may run, in
the chart or the config file, and an enabled node with an empty list is a
startup error rather than a licence to run anything. Same shape as the
discovery CIDR allowlist and for the same reason: the permissive reading of
an empty list is how a deliberately narrow capability becomes a shell.

The allowlist matches on the resolved absolute path, not on the string the
flow typed. Comparing strings would let a flow name "curl" and get whichever
curl is first on the PATH of the process — and PATH is something a Function
node can read and a sidecar can influence. Symlinks are evaluated too, so
two spellings of the same binary compare equal in both directions.

There is no shell. The command line is split on quoting rules only, and an
unquoted metacharacter is refused rather than passed through as a literal —
a flow author who typed a pipe meant a pipe, and running the command with a
literal "|" argument would do something they did not ask for while looking
like it worked. The appended message property is one argument, never split,
because splitting it lets a payload arriving over MQTT decide how many
arguments the command gets.

Refusal happens at deploy time as well as per message, so a flow naming a
forbidden command fails in front of whoever deployed it rather than at 3am.
A command that was not on the PATH at boot is kept rather than rejected and
resolved again on use — an init container or a mounted volume supplying it
later is a deployment ordering problem, not a configuration error.

Two more bounds Node-RED does not have. Output is capped per stream and the
truncation raises an error, because a flow acting on half a result believing
it has all of it is worse than no result; Node-RED buffers without a limit,
so `cat` on the wrong file takes the pod. And concurrency is bounded, so a
node whose command takes a minute cannot accumulate a process per message.

Both buffered and streaming modes, all three outputs, msg.rc on every one of
them, and the timeout. A command that forks children of its own may leave
them behind when it is killed — that is written into the compatibility notes
rather than left for someone to discover. Fixing it properly needs process
groups, which are per-platform, and _linux in a filename has already cost
this codebase a day.

Tests run the test binary as its own subject, which is the standard library's
own pattern for os/exec and the only portable one: no command exists with the
same name and behaviour on both a Windows workstation and a distroless image.

title: XML, YAML and HTML parsers, and a CSS selector engine to go with them
body:
YAML is the easy one: the same shape as the JSON node, toggling on the
value's type, sharing the decoder normalisation the Template node already
needed. yaml.v3 hands back int where everything else in the runtime is a
float64 that came through encoding/json, and a Switch node comparing an int
against 1883 does not match. That conversion is now in one place.

XML follows xml2js's object convention, because that is what an imported
flow will be indexing into: attributes under $, element text under _, and
every child element an array. The array part is xml2js's explicitArray
default and it is the one people find surprising, so ew_explicitArray turns
it off — with the warning in the help text that collapsing a single child
reads better right up until a second one appears and the shape changes under
the flow.

A leaf with no attributes decodes to its text rather than to {_: text}. That
is a judgement call: it makes payload.reading[0] work instead of
payload.reading[0]._, which is what anyone writing the flow expects, and it
matches what xml2js does.

msg.options is refused rather than ignored. Node-RED passes it straight
through to xml2js, and those options change the shape of the output — a flow
setting mergeAttrs and getting an object without it gets a different object,
not a slightly different one.

HTML needed a CSS selector engine, and x/net/html was already in the tree as
an indirect dependency so the parser was free. The engine covers type, id,
class, attribute with the four string operators, descendant, child and comma
groups, which is what an HTML node is actually used for: reading a device's
status page because it has no API, which on a plant floor is most of them.

Everything else is refused at deploy time. That is the part worth arguing
about, so: a selector engine that silently drops :nth-child matches more
elements than the selector says and keeps working. A flow reading the wrong
meter for a month is a worse outcome than a deploy that fails immediately
with the reason. Same for the ~= and |= attribute operators, sibling
combinators and namespaces.

Two bugs found writing the tests, both the same shape — checking the
supported case before the unsupported one. [lang|=en] parsed as a plain
equality against an attribute named "lang|", which matches nothing, forever,
quietly. And splitting the chain on whitespace treated a > inside an
attribute value as a child combinator. Both now scan with bracket depth
instead of splitting strings.

Returned HTML is re-rendered from the parse tree, so it is normalised markup
rather than the original bytes. Written into the compatibility notes, because
a flow comparing the result against a stored string will not match the first
time a source page changes its formatting.

36 node types. Race detector clean.

title: File, File In and Watch, scoped to the PVC
body:
Same argument as the exec node, one notch less severe. Node-RED's file nodes
take any path at all, so "can edit a flow" means "can read any file this
process can read and write any file it can write" — including a mounted
Secret. On a Pi in a workshop that is fine. In an App Store app where the
editor is behind a dashboard login, it is not.

So the file nodes are scoped. Unlike exec this is on by default rather than
off, because the two are not the same kind of thing: reading and writing
files under your own PVC is the ordinary use of the node, whereas running a
command never is. The data directory is always allowed and the operator adds
roots on top of it. Refusing everything by default would have made the nodes
useless out of the box and every operator would have widened the scope to /
just to get started, which is worse than no scope at all because it would
look deliberate.

The check resolves symlinks, which is the part that actually matters. The
hole it closes: a flow writes a file under the PVC, symlinks it to /, and
reads through the link. The textual path still starts with the data
directory, so a string prefix check lets it straight through. Resolving over
the longest existing prefix and re-appending the rest is what makes the same
check work for a write to a file that does not exist yet.

Both read and write are bounded. Node-RED reads a whole file into memory with
no limit, so pointing File In at the wrong path is an OOM-kill rather than an
error; past the cap this says which limit was hit and that per-line or
chunked mode would work. A raw read produces ImmutableBytes, so fanning a
large file across several wires shares the buffer instead of copying it per
wire — that is the entire reason the type exists and this is its best case.

Writes are fsynced by default, which Node-RED's are not. This node is what a
flow uses to log to the PVC, and a log that loses its last hour to a power
cut is not a log. It is a property, so anyone who would rather have the
throughput can have it.

Watch polls instead of using the kernel's notification interface. That is a
deliberate trade and it is in the compatibility notes: a change is seen
within the poll interval rather than immediately, and two changes inside one
interval are reported once. fsnotify means per-platform code and a filename
suffix that is a build constraint, and _js in a filename has already cost
this codebase a day by silently removing the Function node from every build.
The first pass records what is already there without emitting, so starting a
flow does not announce every existing file as new, and the walk is capped so
a recursive watch on a large tree cannot stall the runtime.

title: HTTP In, HTTP Response and HTTP Request, and a router that can forget
body:
The admin API and the editor are a ServeMux built once at start-up. Flow
routes cannot be: they appear and disappear on every deploy, and ServeMux has
no way to remove a pattern. So internal/flowhttp, which the API server
delegates to for anything the fixed routes did not claim.

Three rules in the router, all of them refusals, all for the same reason —
the alternative fails without saying anything.

Two nodes claiming the same method and path is refused at deploy. Express
runs whichever matched first and the second node simply never fires, and
nothing anywhere tells you which one won.

A path that would shadow the editor or the admin API is refused. The symptom
otherwise is an editor that stops loading, from a change nobody would connect
to it.

Routes are ordered by specificity, per segment: literal beats parameter beats
wildcard. Without it, whether /api/health reaches the health endpoint or the
/api/:id node depends on the order the nodes happened to start in, which is
map iteration order, which is deliberately random.

HTTP In builds the same msg.req / msg.res / msg.payload shape Node-RED does —
JSON, form-encoded and raw bodies, :params, trailing *, lower-cased header
names because that is what Node's http module produces and what an imported
flow indexes into. msg.req.rawBody keeps the exact bytes alongside the
decoded payload, because a signature check needs them and re-encoding the
decoded form does not reproduce them.

msg.res is a plain struct, which is what makes it survive Msg.Clone: the
clone's default branch shares values it does not recognise. Both branches of
a fan-out therefore hold the same response, and a sync.Once turns the second
reply into a reported error instead of a panic on a closed connection.
Node-RED discards the second reply silently, so half the response the flow
believes it sent never existed.

A request nobody answers is closed with 504 after a timeout. Node-RED holds
it open forever, so a flow missing the Response node leaks a connection per
request until the process runs out of sockets and stops answering — with
nothing in the log. The handler goroutine blocks until the reply lands, which
it has to: returning would let net/http recycle the ResponseWriter while the
flow still holds it.

HTTP Request bounds the response size and the call, neither of which Node-RED
does, and fills {{mustache}} in the URL from the message. A non-2xx is data
rather than an error, matching Node-RED — a flow polling an endpoint that
404s while a device boots wants a Switch node, not a Catch. There is no
egress allowlist and I am not adding one: this node can reach anything the
pod can, exactly as Node-RED's can, and the place to bound that is a
NetworkPolicy rather than an edit dialog nobody outside the cluster can
trust. That is in the compatibility notes rather than left implied.

One pre-existing bug fixed on the way past. The link registry was never
reset, so a deleted Link In stayed registered holding the emitter of a
runtime that had stopped, and a Link Out in the new flow still naming it
delivered into a dead runner. Both process-wide registries are cleared when
a runtime stops now.

42 node types. helm lint clean, race detector clean.

title: WebSocket, TCP and UDP: the last of the palette
body:
Nine nodes, and the compatibility list is now complete except for subflow
instances.

WebSocket listeners share the flow route table with the HTTP In nodes, which
falls out of building the router first and is the right answer anyway: a
websocket path cannot shadow the editor and cannot silently collide with an
HTTP endpoint. There is a test for exactly that, because it is the kind of
thing that works until the day somebody reuses a path.

The one real design decision is what a websocket does when a client stops
reading. Node-RED queues without limit. Here the frame is refused to a Catch
node and the connection is closed. Blocking instead would push back-pressure
from a slow browser all the way into the flow's scheduler, and a tab left
open on a laptop lid must not be able to affect a production line — the same
rule the editor's own event channel already follows.

Whole-message mode refuses a frame that is not a JSON object rather than
quietly delivering it as a payload. The node is configured for whole
messages; downgrading silently makes every property the flow reads come back
undefined, which reads as a broken flow rather than a broken frame.

TCP In does stream and single mode with a real multi-byte delimiter — a
plant-floor protocol is as likely to terminate on ETX or a null as on a
newline, and bufio.ScanLines only knows about the latter. Every message
carries msg._session so TCP Out can reply on the connection it arrived on;
that needs a process-wide registry for the same reason the Link nodes do, the
two nodes may be on different tabs with nothing in the graph joining them.

Three bounds Node-RED does not have, all of them the same failure: accepted
connections, the size of one delimited message, and the total of a
single-mode read. A peer that opens connections and never closes them, or
sends without ever sending the delimiter, otherwise grows the heap until the
pod dies with nothing to point at.

TCP Request implements all four wait modes. Every request opens its own
connection — Node-RED's connection-reuse mode is not implemented, and it is
not an oversight: all four wait modes end at a connection boundary, so
reusing one changes what "the reply" means. That is in the notes rather than
left for someone to find.

UDP In joins a multicast group on a named interface, which matters in macvlan
mode where the pod has more than one and the kernel's first pick is not the
OT VLAN. UDP Out keeps one socket rather than opening one per message; a per
message socket burns an ephemeral port per datagram and exhausts the range in
minutes on a busy flow.

A byte array payload goes on the wire as bytes, not as its JSON. That is how
a Function node hands over a Modbus or EtherNet/IP frame it built, and
getting it wrong would put "[0,1,255]" on a PLC's socket.

51 node types. Race detector clean across every package on Linux with cgo.

title: Subflows run
body:
They parsed, round-tripped and rendered for sixteen commits and did nothing.
Now an instance is a real copy of its template's nodes, wired to the
instance's own neighbours, with its own flow context and its own resolved
properties.

The expansion produces a separate graph rather than rewriting the parsed
flows. That is the whole design decision and it buys two things. The flow
file is untouched, so the byte-identical round-trip still holds — an
expansion that mutated Flows in place would replace a customer's tidy subflow
with its inlined guts on the first deploy, permanently. And the expanded
graph is an ordinary graph, so the scheduler, the Catch routing, the metrics
and the editor's status events all work inside a subflow with no special
cases at all. Flows.Expanded refuses to marshal, so the graph that runs can
never be mistaken for the graph that saves.

An instance's scope id is the instance node's id. That gives each instance
its own flow context — two instances of a counting subflow must not share a
counter — and it is stable across deploys, which matters because context is
keyed by node id and a fresh id every deploy would silently reset a
subflow's state.

Environment resolution is the part that makes subflows worth having. A node
inside an instance resolves against the instance's own properties, then the
template's defaults, then the properties of whatever instance contains that
one, out to the tab and finally the process. Without the chain, subflow
properties are decoration and every instance behaves identically. A property
typed "env" is an indirection and deliberately does not resolve in its own
frame — that is how a nested subflow forwards a value it was handed without
knowing it.

Proved end to end rather than in a unit test: one template, two instances,
one overriding UNIT and one not, deployed through the API and writing to a
file. 4.2 bar and 4.2 kPa.

Three judgement calls written into the code:

An error nobody caught inside a subflow walks out to the calling flow, and
the handler is chosen against the instance node so the group-distance rule
applies where the subflow actually sits. A Catch inside the subflow still
wins — the author who handled it there meant to. Without the walk, a subflow
is where errors go to disappear.

A configuration node declared inside a template is shared by every instance
rather than copied. An MQTT broker inside a subflow is an author saying
"share this"; copying it opens a connection per instance against something
that is probably counting them.

A template declaring more than one input gets a warning, because a v1 wire
names a target node and not a target port, so the second one is unreachable.
Delivering to the first and staying quiet would look correct.

`emberwire import` now counts against the expanded graph. A subflow whose
internals need a node this build does not have used to report as one clean
"subflow instance"; it now says which node type is missing and how many
copies of it there are, which is the difference between finding out now and
finding out when a line stops.

Race detector clean.

title: emberwire bench, and the comparison it was gating
body:
The README has said "still not benchmarked against Node-RED" since the first
commit, because the figures people quote for Node-RED are anecdotes —
different hardware, different flows, different Node versions, nothing
controlled — and repeating one with our name on it would be passing a rumour
off as a measurement. So here is the harness, and here are the numbers it
produced.

Two modes, because they answer different questions. Engine mode pushes
messages through a chain of real Change nodes with no I/O in the path and
reports messages per second, nanoseconds per message and bytes allocated per
message: the scheduler and the message model and nothing else. HTTP mode
drives an endpoint a flow answers, at a fixed concurrency, and reports
throughput and latency percentiles. HTTP mode does not know or care which
runtime is on the other end, which is exactly what makes it fair.

The chain is built from real Change nodes rather than a purpose-built
benchmark node. A synthetic node that did nothing would measure the scheduler
and flatter it; this pays for the same property expressions, the same clone
on every hop, the same inbox and the same goroutine handoff a flow does.

The load generator is closed-loop — each client sends the next request when
the last came back. That measures what the far end can absorb and cannot
produce the coordinated-omission latency an open-loop generator reports once
the target falls behind. The warm-up is discarded; Node's JIT needs one and
it costs nothing to be even-handed.

One bug worth recording because of how it presented. Every client is
mid-request when the deadline lands, so every one of them left through the
cancelled-request branch — and the sample slice was assigned after the loop,
which no client ever reached. The latency percentiles printed 0.00 ms. That
does not read as "no data", it reads as a very fast runtime, which is the
worst possible failure mode for a benchmark and the reason it is now a
deferred assignment with a comment saying so.

The run: both runtimes as containers in rootless podman on one box, the same
five-node flow file deployed to each unchanged — it is Node-RED v1 and we
read it as-is, so there is no translation step to argue about — driven by the
same generator in the same session.

  image        25.1 MB vs 717 MB
  idle RSS     4.8 MB  vs 54.6 MB
  under load   12.3 MB vs 179.6 MB
  throughput   3,460   vs 1,290 req/s
  p50 latency  1.03 ms vs 4.61 ms
  p99 latency  16.72   vs 23.14 ms
  cold start   2.1-2.3 vs 4.6-5.5 s

Three caveats are in the README next to the table rather than buried in the
method, because a number without them is a number somebody will misuse. Cold
start includes about two seconds of container start that both pay, so the
runtime difference is the delta and not the ratio. The throughput figure
includes the HTTP stack deliberately — it is the only surface both present
identically — so it is not a measurement of either scheduler alone. And the
p99 gap is far narrower than the p50 gap, because under saturation both
runtimes queue and queueing dominates the tail; the median is where the
per-request cost actually shows.

The README's "450MB image" was wrong. nodered/node-red:latest measured 717MB
pulled today. If a claim is in the README it has to be true today, so it now
says 717, and the number came from `podman images` rather than from memory.

Method, exact commands, flow file and caveats in docs/bench/.

title: Publish on version tags only
body:
Both publish workflows built on every push to main. That is how you end up
with an image in the registry that nobody can name: it exists, something on a
plant floor can be running it, and there is no version anybody can say out
loud. Same for the chart — packaged off a branch it carries whatever
Chart.yaml happened to say, so two different charts can claim one version and
the index quietly serves the second.

Tags only now, `v*`, on both. Three changes beyond the trigger:

The image no longer publishes a branch tag or a bare sha tag. Both produce
artefacts that are not a release. Semver only — {{version}}, major.minor,
major.

The chart is packaged with --version and --app-version taken from the tag
rather than from the committed Chart.yaml. The tag becomes the single source
of truth for what a release is called, so the chart and the image it
references cannot disagree. Chart.yaml's numbers are now marked as
placeholders, because a committed version that drifts from the tag is exactly
the second answer to the same question that causes this.

workflow_dispatch takes an existing tag as input instead of building the
branch, so the manual path cannot produce an untagged build either. And both
jobs re-check the ref shape before doing any work — the trigger already
restricts it, but a future edit to the trigger would silently start
publishing untagged artefacts again and a registry does not forget.

CI stays on push and pull_request. Tests on every commit is right; artefacts
on every commit is not.

title: CI could not build a fresh clone at all
body:
The badge I just put in the README was red, and it was red for a reason that
had been there the whole time: web/embed.go has //go:embed all:dist, web/dist
is a build artefact, and the root .gitignore excluded the directory outright.
A clone of this repo could not run go build, go vet or go test — every one of
them failed with "pattern all:dist: no matching files found". It only ever
worked on my box because my dist was sitting there from an editor build.

The comment above that embed has always said "the placeholder file keeps this
compiling before the editor has been built". web/.gitignore was already
written for it — dist/* with !dist/.gitkeep, exactly right. The root
.gitignore said /web/dist/ and won, and git will not re-include a file inside
an excluded directory, so the placeholder the design assumed could never
exist. Root now excludes the contents rather than the directory, and the
placeholder is committed.

The static-build job now builds the real editor before compiling. It reports
the binary size and enforces the 40 MiB budget, and doing that against a
binary carrying a 200-byte placeholder would report a size that is not the
shipped one and pass a budget it was never tested against.

And it asserts the bundle actually got embedded, because web.Assets falls
back to a plain-text explanation when it is missing — the right thing at
runtime and the wrong thing to ship without noticing. The marker is
dark-mode-pending, the FOUC guard from the built index.html: not in any Go
source, impossible to be present unless the real bundle was embedded.
Verified against a locally built binary rather than assumed.

title: Handoff: the lessons from shipping it
body:
Five things that cost time this session and would cost it again.

A fresh clone could not build, and had not been able to for twenty-three
commits. //go:embed all:dist plus a root .gitignore excluding /web/dist/
meant go build, go vet and go test all failed on any machine that had not run
the editor build. It only ever worked on mine because dist was sitting there.
The rule worth keeping: git will not re-include a file inside an excluded
directory — exclude the contents, never the directory. And clone into /tmp and
build before believing an embed works.

GitHub Pages is not enabled by pushing to gh-pages. The chart workflow went
green and the index still 404'd. It is one API call per repo, and a green
publish job is not proof the index resolves. curl it.

Publishing is tag-only now, which also means pushing to main is safe — CI runs
and nothing is published. Worth knowing before hesitating over a push.

Git Bash rewrites a leading slash into a Windows path. -path /bench became
C:/Program Files/Git/bench and looked like a server that would not answer.

And the one I am least pleased about: I wrote a CI check that grepped the
binary for "emberwire-editor" to prove the editor was embedded. No such string
exists anywhere. It would have passed forever while checking nothing. Find a
real string in the real artefact and prove it matches before committing the
check.

Also recorded: the dashboard is the blocker now, not this repo — an invited
user gets 403'd on every scoped route because the invite flow never writes a
tenant binding, so they sign in and see nothing, Emberwire included. And a
short section on working in that tree: not gofmt-clean, git add -A sweeps up
work in progress, main is protected so a push cannot be taken back.

title: A credentials file from Emberwire 0.1.0 now says what it is
body:
2.0.0 fails to start on a credentials file written by 0.1.0, and the message
was "parsing decrypted credentials: json: cannot unmarshal string into Go value
of type map[string]string". That is the plaintext parser choking on an
encrypted envelope, and it tells the operator nothing about what to do.

An encrypted file carries its format as a string, and a plaintext file cannot,
because every value in it is an object keyed by node id. So a string format
that is not ours is now refused by name. For 0.1.0's, the error says the file
was written by Emberwire 0.1.0, that 2 cannot read it, and to move it aside and

title: Fix the chart's generated admin password, which never matched its hash
body:
The chart generates an admin password, stores it in the Secret, and the install
notes print how to read it. The login it printed never worked. This is from
0.1.0 through 2.0.1, and it was found by installing the published chart on a
live k3s cluster and logging in with the password the chart had stored.

adminPasswordHash called adminPassword a second time, and on a first install,
when there is no Secret to read back, each call drew its own random password.
So the stored hash was a hash of one password and the stored password was
another. Rendering the chart twice and diffing it could not show this, because
both values are random, and CI never rendered the chart before a tag.

The hash is now made from the password the Secret is being written with, which
the caller passes in. An existing hash is kept, so an upgrade does not rotate
it, only when the Secret carries a marker annotation and its stored password is
still the one being written. A Secret written before the marker existed is
made again once from its stored password, which is what fixes a release that
was installed with the bug, in place, without changing the password or the
credential secret.

CI now has a chart job: helm lint, and a bcrypt check that the generated
password matches its hash, three times because it is random, plus a stated
password and an explicit hash.

Run on the Fragua k3s cluster with the packaged chart: a release installed with
the bug went from 401 to 200 on upgrade with the password and credential secret
unchanged, a fresh install logged in, a second upgrade left the Secret alone,
and a flow deployed through the API survived a pod restart. The first upgrade
after an install still restarts the pod once, because the checksum annotation
re-renders the Secret with fresh randomness. That was already true and is not
changed here.

body:
* HOTLOOP_FLOW_INSECURE=true actually turns auth off now

It never did. The variable set auth.enabled to false and Validate refused a
disabled config no matter how it got that way, then printed a refusal telling
you to set the variable you had just set. From 0.1.0 until today. Nothing
caught it because internal/config had no tests at all.

Validate now knows the difference: the opt-out is its own field, set only by
the environment, so a ConfigMap that says enabled: false still refuses on its
own. With it set you need no users, but a user you do list still gets its hash
checked, and the credential secret still has its own opt-out. Every boot logs
a warning that says what you turned off.

Starting was only half of it. The editor never asked the server whether it
needed a login, so it went straight to a login screen with no users behind it,
and the live event stream refused to open without a token. It asks /settings
first now, which says whether auth is on, the stream connects without a token
when none is needed, and Sign out becomes a "no login" badge.

internal/config gets its first tests, and four of them fail on the old
Validate. Driven end to end in a browser against the built binary, both ways.

* Chart: discovery stops handing out NET_RAW and NET_ADMIN

Turning discovery on added both, for "ARP sweeps" that were never written.
scan only makes TCP connections and netinfo only reads the interface list,
neither needs a capability, so the pod got privilege for nothing. Every render
drops ALL now, discovery or not, and CI fails if a capability gets added back.

The README says both fixes instead of warning about the bugs.

title: Flow tests stand in for the outside world (#38)
body:
A test that ran your MQTT Out for real would publish to the plant's
broker, and then it isn't a test, it's a deploy. So under a test every
node that talks outside the process gets a stand-in: MQTT, HTTP,
PostgreSQL, InfluxDB, TCP, UDP, WebSocket, the file nodes, exec, scan and
netinfo. The node still does its whole job up to the wire, the topic, the
rendered URL, the SQL and its parameters, the line protocol, and hands it
to the stand-in, which records it and answers with whatever the test
scripted. Sources don't subscribe, listen or poll.

A test checks what would have gone out with sent:, scripts what comes
back with replies:, and scripts the historian being down with error:.

The proof points every one of those nodes at a TCP port, a UDP port and a
directory the test holds, runs a reading through all of them, checks
every byte each would have sent, then counts: no connections, no
datagrams, no files, nothing executed. A node that reaches out with no
stand-in is refused by name, and the palette test fails if anybody adds
one.

title: Flow tests keep their own clock (#42)
body:
Nobody runs a suite that waits out a five-minute Delay, so a test doesn't
wait. Every node that waits, Delay, Trigger, Inject on an interval, once
or on a crontab, Join and Batch timeouts and Link Call, now asks its
services for a clock. In a flow it's the wall clock and nothing changes.
Under a test it's one the test moves straight to the next timer, letting
the flow settle after each one, so the order is the order the real
minutes would have made. Five minutes of Delay is one step.

at: puts an injection at a moment on that clock, clock: says when the
test starts so a crontab at half past six can be tested at half past
six, and within and timeout are on it too. A Function node's Date and a
date-typed value read the same clock, so a flow that stamps times agrees
with itself.

Every timing node is proven against it to the millisecond, an hour of
plant time included, in well under a second.

title: Flow tests start from context and credentials they name (#44)
body:
Every test starts with empty context, so a test that needs a counter at
41 says so with context:, and an expectation can say what context holds
at the end, matched like msg, with null meaning not set. A failure says
what the scope does hold, because the usual answer is a typo. Three tests
in a row prove one never starts where the last one stopped.

Credentials are the test's own, by node name or id, and never the real
ones. They reach a node the way real ones would: the password shows up
in the Authorization header the HTTP request would have sent, an
InfluxDB config that needs a token starts with the test's, and a node
pointing at a mounted secret file gets the test's credential instead of
the disk.

Context is in memory, the same store a flow uses today. No file format:
persistent context is going to SQLite.
